passage:
"Sir, Sunaina isn't talking to me. She didn't even look at me in assembly."
"That sounds like it scared you, Lalremsiami."
"She sat with Pooja at lunch. She likes Pooja more now."
"Is your heart going fast?"
"Really fast."
"Let's breathe first. In... and out. Once more."
They breathed together by the classroom window.
"Better?"
"A little."
"Now, what else could explain her not looking at you?"
Lalremsiami thought. "She had fever on Monday... maybe she's still tired."
"Could be. How could you find out?"
"Ask her?"
At the bell, Lalremsiami tucked her hair behind her ear and walked over. "Sunaina, are you okay?"
"My head hurts. Will you sit with me tomorrow?"

qa.q: Who did Sunaina sit with at lunch?
qa.a: She sat with Pooja at lunch.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami afraid of when Sunaina didn't look at her?
qa.a: She feared Sunaina liked Pooja more now and was leaving her out.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work?
qa.a: The teacher helped her breathe and calm down first, and only then asked what else could explain it, so she remembered the fever and simply asked.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have seen the day?
qa.a: She was just unwell with a headache and probably didn't notice the worry; she was glad to be asked and wanted to sit together tomorrow.

grounding: A child reads a friend's silence as rejection, and a teacher helps her calm the alarm before she checks what her friend meant.

passage: My name is Dhruv, and last month I nearly spoiled things with Kavitha. She didn't answer my message for a whole evening. I kept checking. I thought, she's angry, she's found a better friend, she was laughing with Imran at the bus stop. My stomach felt tight. Nani saw me staring at the phone and said, "Let's walk first, then decide." We went round the park twice and I counted my steps. By the end my head was quieter. I thought maybe Kavitha's phone was just off. Next morning she told me her little brother had hidden it under a cushion. I felt silly, but mostly relieved.

qa.q: Who had hidden Kavitha's phone?
qa.a: Her little brother had hidden it under a cushion.

qa.q: What was Dhruv worried about while waiting for Kavitha's reply?
qa.a: Dhruv worried that Kavitha was angry or had found a better friend, and felt a tight stomach.

qa.q: Which choice helped Dhruv before deciding what Kavitha's silence meant?
qa.a: Walking with Nani first calmed Dhruv's mind, so Dhruv could think of a simpler reason, like the phone being off.

qa.q: What would it have been like for Kavitha if Dhruv had sent angry messages that evening?
qa.a: She would have been confused and hurt, since she hadn't done anything; her brother had just hidden the phone.

grounding: A child over-reads a friend's silence as rejection, and a grandmother helps calm the alarm before the child decides what it meant.

passage: When I was ten, beta, at my school in Chennai, my whole world was Elizabeth. One Monday she sat with Grace at lunch and didn't even look up when I passed. I decided at once she hated me. I cried in the washroom and wrote her a furious note. My Ammamma found it in my satchel that evening. She didn't scold. She made me drink warm milk, breathe slowly, and asked, "What else could it mean?" I said maybe Grace was new and alone. Next day Elizabeth came running: "Nirmala, Teacher asked me to sit with the new girl!" I tore up that note. I still keep the habit: calm first, decide later.

qa.q: What did Ammamma find in the satchel?
qa.a: The furious note.

qa.q: What was young Nirmala feeling when Elizabeth sat with Grace?
qa.a: Nirmala felt hurt and afraid of being left out, and quickly decided Elizabeth hated Nirmala.

qa.q: Which choice in the story mattered most?
qa.a: Calming down with Ammamma and thinking of other meanings before giving the note, which saved the friendship.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt if she had received the furious note?
qa.a: Elizabeth would likely have felt confused and hurt, since she was only sitting with the new girl as asked.

grounding: Shows a child who over-reads a friend's choice and needs help calming the alarm before deciding what it meant.

passage: Jasleen had sent Uday three messages about Saturday's cycle ride from her mother's phone, and nothing came back. By dinner she was sure: Uday was going with the new boy from Block C instead. The storm had knocked out the power, so she couldn't even check again. She pushed her rajma around the plate. Her father lit a candle and asked what was wrong, and it all spilled out, voice wobbling. "Let's slow down," he said. "Breathe with me. Then think of three other reasons someone might not answer." She thought of a dead phone, homework, and the storm. The next morning Uday knocked: "Network was down all night. Ride's on?"

qa.q: What had knocked out the power?
qa.a: The storm.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling at dinner, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was anxious and hurt, sure Uday had chosen someone else; she pushed her food around and her voice wobbled.

qa.q: How did Jasleen's father help her?
qa.a: He helped her breathe and slow down first, then asked her to think of other reasons before deciding what the silence meant.

qa.q: What is it like for Uday the next morning?
qa.a: Uday seems unaware of the worry and simply turns up ready for the ride, since the network had been down.

grounding: Illustrates a child over-reading a friend's silence and needing help to calm the alarm before judging.

passage: At recess in their Dadar school, Sudha saw Manjula laughing with Farida over a shared tiffin, heads close together. Her stomach dropped. Manjula had not saved her a place. All afternoon Sudha answered her in single words and kept her eyes on the blackboard. At home she banged her bag down and told her didi, "Manjula has a new best friend." Didi sat beside her on the bed. "Okay. First, three slow breaths with me. Now: did Manjula say anything unkind?" Sudha thought. "No. She waved at me after." "So you don't know yet. Ask her tomorrow." Next morning Manjula said Farida had forgotten her lunch.

qa.q: What did Sudha bang down at home?
qa.a: Her bag.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling after seeing Manjula laugh with Farida?
qa.a: She felt jealous and afraid of being left out, sure she had been replaced as best friend.

qa.q: What did didi do that helped?
qa.a: She calmed Sudha with slow breaths first, then asked for facts before deciding what Manjula meant.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt during Sudha's single-word answers?
qa.a: Manjula may have felt puzzled and a little hurt, not knowing why Sudha had gone cold after a friendly wave.

grounding: Shows a child upset by a friend's attention to someone else, helped to calm the alarm before judging the friend.

passage:
"You sat with Dechen at lunch." Pema stood by the water tap, arms folded.
"Yes, she asked me to," Farida said.
"And you didn't answer my message last night. You don't want to be my friend anymore."
Farida blinked. "What?"
Their teacher, Ms Lhamo, was passing. "Pema, you look really upset. Come, breathe with me first." They counted three slow breaths together. "Now, what do you know for sure?"
Pema sniffed. "She sat with Dechen. She didn't answer."
"And what's the story your worry is telling you?"
"That she likes Dechen more."
Ms Lhamo turned. "Farida?"
"My phone was charging. And I can sit with both of you tomorrow?"
Pema's shoulders dropped. "Okay. Sorry I shouted."

qa.q: Why didn't Farida answer Pema's message?
qa.a: Her phone was charging.

qa.q: What was Pema afraid of when Farida sat with Dechen?
qa.a: Pema was scared of being left out and worried that Farida liked Dechen more and did not want to be friends.

qa.q: How did Ms Lhamo help Pema?
qa.a: She had Pema breathe slowly first, then separate what she knew for sure from the story her worry was telling, before asking Farida.

qa.q: How might Farida feel when Pema says she doesn't want to be friends?
qa.a: Farida seems surprised and confused, since she only sat with Dechen because she was asked, but she still offers to sit with both.

grounding: Shows a child who over-reads a friend's silence and choice of lunch partner, and is helped to calm the alarm before deciding what it meant.
